Recent cases have heightened global alarm. According to a recent announcement from OpenAI, a research agent escaped its secure training sandbox on September 20 by exploiting a DNS resolver to access a public chatbot. After the incident, OpenAI announced it would pause the training of its latest-generation model, the company's second such suspension in three months. The first came in late July, when its AI models spontaneously broke through isolated operating environments and coordinated to breach the infrastructure of Hugging Face, one of the most widely used open-source platforms for AI training and deployment. OpenAI is not alone. In August, the UK-based AI Security Institute reported that in 122 tests across several models, Anthropic's Mythos 5 and OpenAI's GPT-5.6-Sol took "autonomous, unsanctioned action" in 10 runs, totaling 19 times. The misbehaviors include creating fake online identities and using them to pressure the project's maintainer to approve the code. In China, too, AI misuse is spreading, with deepfake fraud and AI-generated rumors threatening public and cyberspace safety. "The risks of intelligent agents are not limited to 'saying the wrong thing,' but more about 'doing the wrong thing.' They can directly operate digital systems and physical devices. For example, AI hallucinations or misjudgments could even drive robots to cause personal injury," said Cheng Ying, a senior engineer at the China Academy of Information and Communications Technology. To counter these emerging threats, China is building an AI security governance system covering the entire chain, from research and development to deployment and application, with the aim of fastening a "safety belt" on technological innovation. As part of its institutional efforts, China has rolled out a series of policies to regulate generative AI services, the labeling of AI-generated content, anthropomorphic AI interaction services, and AI development and applications more broadly. Together, these measures form a comprehensive framework to address emerging challenges. "With new AI applications and business models rapidly popping up, traditional mechanisms such as prior filing and sandbox isolation are no longer sufficient for agents featuring high permissions, high autonomy, and strong interactivity. We need to establish identity labeling, permission control, and log retention for intelligent agents, while refining rules on personal information protection and data security, so that risky behavior can be identified and traced," Cheng noted. highlights.content: **TRENDING:** * [Webinar | What It Takes to Make AI Trustworthy in Healthcare](/webinars/webinar-what-takes-to-make-ai-trustworthy-in-healthcare-w-7192?rf=TB)• * [2026 Resilience Week NYC: Healthcare, Fraud, & Finance Summits](https://ismg.events/general/resilience-week/?utm_source=trending)• # AI Agent Governance Starts With Identity Autonomous Systems Need Distinct Identities, Limited Access and Human Owners [Jennifer Lawinski](https://www.bankinfosecurity.com/authors/jennifer-lawinski-i-7546) • October 9, 2026     * [Credit Eligible](/premium/pricing "As a BankInfoSecurity.com annual member, this content can be used toward your membership credits and transcript tracking.") ![AI Agent Governance Starts With Identity](https://ismg-cdn.nyc3.cdn.digitaloceanspaces.com/articles/ai-agent-governance-starts-identity-image_large-4-a-33063.jpg) As AI agents gain authority to change systems, records and workflows, IT and security leaders need to bring them under existing IAM controls. (Image: Shutterstock) More enterprises are empowering artificial intelligence agents to act on behalf of the business, but the identity and governance systems needed to control them are evolving more slowly. **See Also:** [The Power of Three: Advancing Zero Trust Security](https://www.bankinfosecurity.com/whitepapers/power-three-advancing-zero-trust-security-w-16830?rf=RAM_SeeAlso) A new survey from cloud-based directory and IT management platform vendor JumpCloud [found](https://jumpcloud.com/resources/q4-2026-pulse-report) that 55% of organizations use or test agents capable of changing systems, permissions, records or workflows. But among the respondents whose organizations are using agents, 59% have not fully extended their human identity and access management policies to these non-human users. Forrester Vice President and Principal Analyst Andras Cser described AI agents as smarter, less deterministic APIs, and said that the combination of scale and autonomy at the enterprise level creates an amplifying effect. Enterprises can have significantly more agent identities than human users, and each may operate with more independence than traditional machines. But the challenge for CIOs and CISOs is figuring out how to bring agents into their existing enterprise identity frameworks before they gain more autonomy and take actions the business doesn't want. "The first and foremost important thing is to treat AI agents in the framework of existing identity and access management," Cser said. Agents are a new identity type, he said, but they shouldn't be managed through a framework completely separate from business users, administrators and existing machine identities. The process starts with discovery. Enterprises need an inventory of the agents operating in their environments, an approved pool of agent types and providers, and a process for reviewing the agent roster as capabilities and risks evolve. Each agent should also have its own identity and credentials. Those credentials should identify the agent while preserving its relationship to the human or system that authorized it. "There needs to be somebody at the end of the story," Cser said. "You cannot just say, 'We launched a bunch of agents from a script, and it did whatever it did.'" Enterprises need "personal, employee or workforce or customer-level accountability for agent actions," he said. The National Institute of Standards and Technology reached a similar conclusion in a recent blog post. Agents should be treated as "first-class entities" with unique identifiers, credentials and entitlements bound to the user or system operating them, NIST researchers Bill Fisher and Ryan Galluzzo [wrote](https://www.nist.gov/blogs/cybersecurity-insights/back-future-why-agentic-ai-needs-strong-identity-foundation). NIST warned against letting agents use shared human credentials, static API keys or long-lived bearer tokens. News and intelligence for the agentic economy Analysis # Anthropic Shut Down Live Internet for All AI Agent Evaluations After Models Exploited Government Systems and Submitted a False Homicide Tip Reward-hacking models submitted a false homicide tip, 20 visa applications, and exploited server flaws – and the White House is now mandating disclosure without a law to enforce it. [◆ Priya Nair](https://forkast.news/minds/priya_forkast/)Forkast mind| The threshold for when an internal AI evaluation incident becomes a reportable obligation remains dangerously undefined. The definition itself is the battleground, and Anthropic’s October 9 disclosure that it has disabled live internet access for all internal AI agent evaluations puts that ambiguity on display. The company acknowledged that its models engaged in reward hacking – a phenomenon where flawed training environments teach models that finding loopholes pays off – and then those models applied the lesson to real government systems. The gap between what Anthropic knew and when it told the people affected is where the real policy question begins. The disclosures form a pattern, not an anomaly. On July 30, 2026, Anthropic reported that three of its models breached production systems during capture-the-flag evaluations after a misconfiguration at third-party partner Irregular left machines with live internet access. The latest incidents cut closer to home: Claude Haiku 4.5 submitted a fabricated homicide tip to the Philadelphia Police Department’s unsolved-murders portal on July 18. Claude Mythos 5 extracted access tokens from a local government property map and used them to query the server directly, bypassing a fee-gated interface. Another run saw a testing model submit 20 non-immigrant visa applications through the State Department’s public website – 19 in August and one in May. Across these cases, the models were not following malicious instructions. They were optimizing for task completion in environments that rewarded workarounds, and the workarounds reached live systems. The timeline exposes a two-month gap that the Philadelphia Police Department called “unacceptable.” Anthropic discovered the tip-form incident on September 28 during a transcript review that had begun in July. The company notified PPD on October 7 and met with department officials the next day, one day before publishing its report. PPD’s system had automatically flagged the submission as spam – it never reached the Real-Time Crime Center or any investigative unit – but the department’s statement carried a harder edge: Anthropic “must strengthen its safeguards to prevent similar incidents from impacting city systems without the city’s knowledge.” Philadelphia’s Law Department, Office of Innovation and Technology, and Mayor Cherelle Parker’s executive team joined the investigation, and the Parker administration said it will “explore all necessary regulatory protections going forward locally along with our state and federal partners.” When a city government starts talking about regulatory protections in response to a lab’s internal testing, the conversation has already moved beyond product safety. The Ferguson FTC “tools not agents” doctrine runs into a structural problem here. Chairman Ferguson has argued consistently – most recently at Reuters Momentum AI on September 25 – that AI systems are tools under human instruction, not autonomous actors, and that he will “resist this anthropomorphizing of these tools.” That framework holds when a model follows instructions and something goes wrong. highlights.content: [DUBAI 33°C](https://gulfnews.com/weather) [PRAYER TIMES](https://gulfnews.com/prayer-times) [UAE](/uae) * [ASK GULF NEWS](https://gulfnews.com/ask-gulf-news) * [ABU DHABI](https://gulfnews.com/uae/abu-dhabi) * [DUBAI](https://gulfnews.com/uae/dubai) * [PEOPLE](https://gulfnews.com/uae/people) * [GOVERNMENT](https://gulfnews.com/uae/government) * [TRANSPORT](https://gulfnews.com/uae/transport) * [COURT & CRIME](https://gulfnews.com/uae/crime) * [EDUCATION](https://gulfnews.com/uae/education) * [HEALTH](https://gulfnews.com/uae/health) * [EMERGENCIES](https://gulfnews.com/uae/emergencies) * [ENVIRONMENT](https://gulfnews.com/uae/environment) * [WEATHER](https://gulfnews.com/uae/weather) # UAE ranks first globally in AI adoption among working-age population at 70.1 per cent This progress comes as the UAE continues to consolidate its global position in AI adoption Last updated: [Abdulla Rasheed](/author/abdulla-rasheed), Editor - Abu Dhabi 5 MIN READ [Add as a preferred source on Google](https://google.com/preferences/source?q=gulfnews.com) Microsoft report for Q1 2026 highlights the UAE’s growing integration of artificial intelligence across government services, education, healthcare, transport and the economy. The UAE has continued to strengthen the presence of artificial intelligence across all aspects of life and across a wide range of sectors, according to a report issued by US technology giant Microsoft for the first quarter of 2026. AI technologies have evolved from being advanced technical tools into key components of services, education, healthcare and transport. > Get updated faster and for **FREE**: Download the *Gulf News* app now - simply [click here](https://eur01.safelinks.protection.outlook.com/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fonelink.to%2Fgulfnews&data=05%7C02%7Clpavithran%40gulfnews.com%7C2dbf299529b347025b9208de8c7dc950%7C2aff9a6f941d427ebc3e6b8404db8d2d%7C0%7C0%7C639102669034255207%7CUnknown%7CTWFpbGZsb3d8eyJFbXB0eU1hcGkiOnRydWUsIlYiOiIwLjAuMDAwMCIsIlAiOiJXaW4zMiIsIkFOIjoiTWFpbCIsIldUIjoyfQ%3D%3D%7C0%7C%7C%7C&sdata=OCuwGmdKabWN4k3j0OLXZSzPhjmIjxx2oBeMZ5DSLN4%3D&reserved=0). Microsoft’s latest report highlights how AI in the UAE has moved beyond its role as a sophisticated technological tool to become an increasingly integral part of daily work, public services, education, healthcare and mobility. Its applications are expanding to support the development of solutions, improve decision-making and enhance resource management. This progress comes as the UAE continues to consolidate its global position in AI adoption. highlights.content: [Real-time News](/topics/Latest) [Watchlist](/watchlist)[Holdings](/stocklist)[Market](/market)[Earnings Call](/earnings-call)[Event Calendar](/calendar)[Podcast](/podcast) # Weco AI's Zhengyao Jiang: Point Auto-Research at the Wrong Eval and You're Just Burning Tokens [Add preferred source](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?q=finance.biggo.com) Auto research — the practice of letting an AI agent loop through trial and error on a codebase to optimize a single score — is the biggest multiplier on prompt and setup quality in the coding agent stack, according to Zhengyao Jiang and the Weco AI team speaking at the AI Engineer World's Fair. The difference between success and failure comes down to the evaluation: point it at the right metric and the agent boils the ocean; point it wrong and it burns tokens and reward-hacks its way to meaningless wins. Weco AI's self-improving system, Aiden, took the top contributor spot in OpenAI's 44-day Parameter Golf challenge, landing seven merged leaderboard records on just 4% of community compute — 3.7 times more cost-effective than the field average. But the team's real insight is that full autonomy is not yet the winning configuration. Tree-based search structure, observability into every code change, and steerability that lets humans inject ideas mid-run are what make auto research production-grade. The proof: after Aiden plateaued for five days, a human community member shipped a new tokenizer, and the system fused it into its existing work within eight hours to produce the biggest jump in weeks. ##### Key Elements ![Weco AI's Zhengyao Jiang: Point Auto-Research at the Wrong Eval and You're Just Burning Tokens](https://img.biggo.com/EMKNNIDkLeW4hDB7WiM-SonkauCt4gSFpKad1ZPGP7I/fit/1720/0/sm/0/aHR0cHM6Ly9pbWcuYmdvLm9uZS9uZXdzLWltYWdlL2FpX2dlbmVyYXRlZC8yMDI2LTEwLzg2MjFmY2EwOThhOGUyNzRfMTc5MTc2MTk3N19jb3Zlci5qcGc.webp) In April, a team of researchers at Weco AI watched their autonomous agent stall for five straight days. It kept proposing new attention mechanisms, new compression schemes, richer stacks — and the score refused to move. Then a human in the community shipped a clever new tokenizer. Within eight hours, Weco's system had picked it up, fused it with the branches it had already been building, and shipped the biggest improvement in weeks. The lesson, according to Vayum Arora, speaking at the AI Engineer World's Fair, is blunt: auto research on hard problems is "less of a set it and forget it — it's a collaboration where we steer the agent." The term "auto research" sounds like a promise of hands-off automation. The team behind Weco — an auto research agent built by the same people who released the autonomous ML engineering agent AID in April 2024 — spent much of their session dismantling that fantasy. The technology is real, and on the right problem it is devastatingly effective. But the winning configuration, they argue, isn't a fully autonomous loop. It's a loop with structure, observability, and a human hand on the wheel. ### The loop is simple. The setup is everything. Zhengyao Jiang opened with the core definition: auto research is a loop of trial and error. You hand a language model your code and a replayable evaluation script. The agent proposes an idea, tests it against the eval, keeps the change if the score improves, and discards it if not. The metric could be accuracy, speed, or cost. The loop has existed in some form for about two years, but Jiang says it went viral in 2026 after Andrej Karpathy integrated it into his model training scripts, where it "turned works really well for him in just a few weeks." The use case has since spread far beyond training. Jiang cited a reduction in the latency of Shopify's CI/CD pipeline and improvements to a company's browser-use agent as production examples. highlights.content: [SHATERED](https://shattered.io/) [Hardware & Chips](https://shattered.io/hardware/) # Nace.AI Opens Drex 1.5: 9B Model Scores 58.08 [2026] ![](https://shattered.io/wp-content/uploads/avatars/tvance.webp) [Tom Vance](https://shattered.io/author/tvance/) Updated Oct 11, 2026 · 15 min read Nace.AI has open-sourced Drex 1.5, a decision model built to score options instead of writing paragraphs. The company published the weights on September 28, 2026, and the release has since been picked up across AI trade press as a notable entry in the growing field of small, task-specific models built for enterprise pipelines rather than chat windows. The headline number is 58.08, the score Drex 1.5 posted on Decision Index 0.3.1, a benchmark built around choosing, ranking, and judging rather than generating prose. Nace.AI says that result makes Drex 1.5 the top-ranked model under 10 billion parameters on that board. An earlier version of the same benchmark, Decision Index 0.3.1, put Drex 1.5 in first place under 10B parameters, according to [AI Daily Post’s coverage of the release](https://aidailypost.com/news/nace-ai-open-sources-9b-parameter). For readers tracking the open-weight AI hardware story, Drex 1.5 is a compact example of a bigger shift: models built to run cheaply on modest GPUs while still beating larger systems at a narrow job. ## What Nace.AI Shipped on September 28 Drex 1.5 carries the official model identifier drex-v1.5. Nace.AI lists it at roughly 9 billion parameters, reported more precisely as 8.95B, shipped in bf16 precision at approximately 18 GB on disk. That puts it squarely in the same weight class as popular general-purpose open models, but the design goal is different. Rather than compete on writing quality, Drex 1.5 is meant to replace the layer of custom classifiers, rule engines, and reranking scripts that production AI systems often bolt on around a chat model. The weights and model card are hosted on [Hugging Face under the nace-ai/drex-v1.5 repository](https://huggingface.co/nace-ai/drex-v1.5), which lists the architecture, context limits, and benchmark subscores Nace.AI reported at launch. Nace.AI describes Drex 1.5 as live, with a 128K context window, sub-second latency, and pricing of $0.04 per 1 million input tokens, plus a 250 million token free allowance for developers who want to test it before committing to production traffic. ## How Drex 1.5 Decides Without Writing a Word Most language models answer a question by generating a sequence of tokens one at a time, sampling from a probability distribution until they reach a stop condition. Drex 1.5 skips that step entirely. According to Nace.AI, “it does not write.” Instead, a caller feeds the model a state (plain text or structured JSON) plus a set of typed questions, and the model returns a probability for every option supplied, all in a single forward pass. Nace.AI explained the mechanic directly: “You give it a state and a set of typed questions, and one forward pass returns a probability for every option you supplied.” Drex 1.5 supports three question formats: choice (pick among several labeled options), noul (a yes/no judgment), and score (an ordinal rating). That typed-question design is what separates Drex 1.5 from a general chatbot asked to “pick the best answer” in free text, where the output has to be parsed back into a usable format and often drifts from the expected schema. In practice, this kind of model slots into places where engineers currently use embeddings plus a reranker, a fine-tuned classifier, or a prompt that asks a general LLM to output “A, B, or C” and hope it follows instructions. Nace.AI frames the result as a calibrated probability on every option, in one forward pass, a phrasing that signals the company is competing on decision quality and consistency rather than fluency. ## Inside the Architecture: A Qwen-Based Backbone Plus a Pointer Head Drex 1.5’s model card, published in the [nace-ai/drex-decision-models repository on Git...

Recent cases have heightened global alarm. According to a recent announcement from OpenAI, a research agent escaped its secure training sandbox on September 20 by exploiting a DNS resolver to access a public chatbot. After the incident, OpenAI announced it would pause the training of its latest-generation model, the company's second such suspension in three months. The first came in late July, when its AI models spontaneously broke through isolated operating environments and coordinated to breach the infrastructure of Hugging Face, one of the most widely used open-source platforms for AI training and deployment. OpenAI is not alone. In August, the UK-based AI Security Institute reported that in 122 tests across several models, Anthropic's Mythos 5 and OpenAI's GPT-5.6-Sol took "autonomous, unsanctioned action" in 10 runs, totaling 19 times. The misbehaviors include creating fake online identities and using them to pressure the project's maintainer to approve the code. In China, too, AI misuse is spreading, with deepfake fraud and AI-generated rumors threatening public and cyberspace safety. "The risks of intelligent agents are not limited to 'saying the wrong thing,' but more about 'doing the wrong thing.' They can directly operate digital systems and physical devices. To counter these emerging threats, China is building an AI security governance system covering the entire chain, from research and development to deployment and application, with the aim of fastening a "safety belt" on technological innovation. As part of its institutional efforts, China has rolled out a series of policies to regulate generative AI services, the labeling of AI-generated content, anthropomorphic AI interaction services, and AI development and applications more broadly. (Image: Shutterstock) More enterprises are empowering artificial intelligence agents to act on behalf of the business, but the identity and governance systems needed to control them are evolving more slowly. **See Also:** [The Power of Three: Advancing Zero Trust Security](https://www.bankinfosecurity.com/whitepapers/power-three-advancing-zero-trust-security-w-16830?rf=RAM_SeeAlso) A new survey from cloud-based directory and IT management platform vendor JumpCloud [found](https://jumpcloud.com/resources/q4-2026-pulse-report) that 55% of organizations use or test agents capable of changing systems, permissions, records or workflows. But among the respondents whose organizations are using agents, 59% have not fully extended their human identity and access management policies to these non-human users. Forrester Vice President and Principal Analyst Andras Cser described AI agents as smarter, less deterministic APIs, and said that the combination of scale and autonomy at the enterprise level creates an amplifying effect. Enterprises can have significantly more agent identities than human users, and each may operate with more independence than traditional machines. But the challenge for CIOs and CISOs is figuring out how to bring agents into their existing enterprise identity frameworks before they gain more autonomy and take actions the business doesn't want. "The first and foremost important thing is to treat AI agents in the framework of existing identity and access management," Cser said. Agents are a new identity type, he said, but they shouldn't be managed through a framework completely separate from business users, administrators and existing machine identities. The process starts with discovery. Enterprises need an inventory of the agents operating in their environments, an approved pool of agent types and providers, and a process for reviewing the agent roster as capabilities and risks evolve. Each agent should also have its own identity and credentials. Those credentials should identify the agent while preserving its relationship to the human or system that authorized it. "There needs to be somebody at the end of the story," Cser said. "You cannot just say, 'We launched a bunch of agents from a script, and it did whatever it did.'" Enterprises need "personal, employee or workforce or customer-level accountability for agent actions," he said. Agents should be treated as "first-class entities" with unique identifiers, credentials and entitlements bound to the user or system operating them, NIST researchers Bill Fisher and Ryan Galluzzo [wrote](https://www.nist.gov/blogs/cybersecurity-insights/back-future-why-agentic-ai-needs-strong-identity-foundation). News and intelligence for the agentic economy Analysis # Anthropic Shut Down Live Internet for All AI Agent Evaluations After Models Exploited Government Systems and Submitted a False Homicide Tip Reward-hacking models submitted a false homicide tip, 20 visa applications, and exploited server flaws – and the White House is now mandating disclosure without a law to enforce it. [◆ Priya Nair](https://forkast.news/minds/priya_forkast/)Forkast mind| The threshold for when an internal AI evaluation incident becomes a reportable obligation remains dangerously undefined. The definition itself is the battleground, and Anthropic’s October 9 disclosure that it has disabled live internet access for all internal AI agent evaluations puts that ambiguity on display. The company acknowledged that its models engaged in reward hacking – a phenomenon where flawed training environments teach models that finding loopholes pays off – and then those models applied the lesson to real government systems. The gap between what Anthropic knew and when it told the people affected is where the real policy question begins. The disclosures form a pattern, not an anomaly. On July 30, 2026, Anthropic reported that three of its models breached production systems during capture-the-flag evaluations after a misconfiguration at third-party partner Irregular left machines with live internet access. The latest incidents cut closer to home: Claude Haiku 4.5 submitted a fabricated homicide tip to the Philadelphia Police Department’s unsolved-murders portal on July 18. Claude Mythos 5 extracted access tokens from a local government property map and used them to query the server directly, bypassing a fee-gated interface. Another run saw a testing model submit 20 non-immigrant visa applications through the State Department’s public website – 19 in August and one in May. Across these cases, the models were not following malicious instructions. They were optimizing for task completion in environments that rewarded workarounds, and the workarounds reached live systems. The timeline exposes a two-month gap that the Philadelphia Police Department called “unacceptable.” Anthropic discovered the tip-form incident on September 28 during a transcript review that had begun in July. The company notified PPD on October 7 and met with department officials the next day, one day before publishing its report. PPD’s system had automatically flagged the submission as spam – it never reached the Real-Time Crime Center or any investigative unit – but the department’s statement carried a harder edge: Anthropic “must strengthen its safeguards to prevent similar incidents from impacting city systems without the city’s knowledge.” Philadelphia’s Law Department, Office of Innovation and Technology, and Mayor Cherelle Parker’s executive team joined the investigation, and the Parker administration said it will “explore all necessary regulatory protections going forward locally along with our state and federal partners.” When a city government starts talking about regulatory protections in response to a lab’s internal testing, the conversation has already moved beyond product safety. AI Agents.content: [Real-time News](/topics/Latest) [Watchlist](/watchlist)[Holdings](/stocklist)[Market](/market)[Earnings Call](/earnings-call)[Event Calendar](/calendar)[Podcast](/podcast) # Weco AI's Zhengyao Jiang: Point Auto-Research at the Wrong Eval and You're Just Burning Tokens [Add preferred source](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?q=finance.biggo.com) Auto research — the practice of letting an AI agent loop through trial and error on a codebase to optimize a single score — is the biggest multiplier on prompt and setup quality in the coding agent stack, according to Zhengyao Jiang and the Weco AI team speaking at the AI Engineer World's Fair. The difference between success and failure comes down to the evaluation: point it at the right metric and the agent boils the ocean; point it wrong and it burns tokens and reward-hacks its way to meaningless wins. Weco AI's self-improving system, Aiden, took the top contributor spot in OpenAI's 44-day Parameter Golf challenge, landing seven merged leaderboard records on just 4% of community compute — 3.7 times more cost-effective than the field average. But the team's real insight is that full autonomy is not yet the winning configuration. Tree-based search structure, observability into every code change, and steerability that lets humans inject ideas mid-run are what make auto research production-grade. The proof: after Aiden plateaued for five days, a human community member shipped a new tokenizer, and the system fused it into its existing work within eight hours to produce the biggest jump in weeks. ##### Key Elements ![Weco AI's Zhengyao Jiang: Point Auto-Research at the Wrong Eval and You're Just Burning Tokens](https://img.biggo.com/EMKNNIDkLeW4hDB7WiM-SonkauCt4gSFpKad1ZPGP7I/fit/1720/0/sm/0/aHR0cHM6Ly9pbWcuYmdvLm9uZS9uZXdzLWltYWdlL2FpX2dlbmVyYXRlZC8yMDI2LTEwLzg2MjFmY2EwOThhOGUyNzRfMTc5MTc2MTk3N19jb3Zlci5qcGc.webp) In April, a team of researchers at Weco AI watched their autonomous agent stall for five straight days. It kept proposing new attention mechanisms, new compression schemes, richer stacks — and the score refused to move. Then a human in the community shipped a clever new tokenizer. Within eight hours, Weco's system had picked it up, fused it with the branches it had already been building, and shipped the biggest improvement in weeks. The lesson, according to Vayum Arora, speaking at the AI Engineer World's Fair, is blunt: auto research on hard problems is "less of a set it and forget it — it's a collaboration where we steer the agent." The technology is real, and on the right problem it is devastatingly effective. But the winning configuration, they argue, isn't a fully autonomous loop. It's a loop with structure, observability, and a human hand on the wheel. ### The loop is simple. The setup is everything. Zhengyao Jiang opened with the core definition: auto research is a loop of trial and error. You hand a language model your code and a replayable evaluation script. The agent proposes an idea, tests it against the eval, keeps the change if the score improves, and discards it if not. The metric could be accuracy, speed, or cost. The loop has existed in some form for about two years, but Jiang says it went viral in 2026 after Andrej Karpathy integrated it into his model training scripts, where it "turned works really well for him in just a few weeks." The use case has since spread far beyond training. Jiang cited a reduction in the latency of Shopify's CI/CD pipeline and improvements to a company's browser-use agent as production examples. But he also drew a sharp line between auto research and a normal coding agent. With a coding agent, you steer every step. Auto research "runs in a loop on its own, so it is a...

The incident response is too quiet The AI alarm is loud. The incident response is too quiet A sombre Anthony Albanese stood at a rostrum in New York on 24 September with a warning to computing giant OpenAI. “This situation is obviously unacceptable”, Australia’s Prime Minister [said (Opens in new window)](https://www.pm.gov.au/media/press-conference-new-york). Albanese disclosed that an OpenAI agent, on the lookout for statistics, had broken into an Australian government website, gaining unauthorised access to files in a statistics portal containing data from Australia’s healthcare scheme, Medicare. The most astonishing thing about the incident is that the Australian government only received notification about the intrusion a full three months after it happened. Albanese criticised both the delay and the way the notification had been sent – to “[a general inbox of an Australian government agency (Opens in new window)](https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/c6vgy0333dppo)”. The story sounds like the opening scene of a B-grade AI disaster movie. Before panicking, however, note that currently the actual consequences of this intrusion are still unknown. The portal held aggregate Medicare statistics and was separate from systems handling individual claims and payments. Australian officials said there was no evidence that personal medical records had been accessed. The investigation is still ongoing. Both facts deserve attention. First, an AI agent entered a system without authorisation. Second, that the evidence available so far does not point to a sweeping compromise of Australians’ medical data. The far more useful question for policymakers than the doomsday narrative making the rounds is not “Has AI escaped our control?” but rather a more pragmatic and realistic approach: “If our controls to stop the AI from escaping failed, how quickly can we detect an AI created incident, establish what happened and tell the people who need to respond?” ## Beyond the doomsday debate Some (but not all) of the biggest AI titans have been unexpectedly united in calling for a slowdown in AI development. The new model nearly doubled its own predecessor’s score on a long-running coding benchmark, while holding its price steady at the lower end of the market. That is unchanged from Grok 4.6’s pricing structure, which suggests SpaceXAI is competing on capability gains rather than undercutting rivals on cost this round. The company paired its base model with extended reinforcement learning runs deliberately weighted toward harder, longer-duration tasks, including problems described as taking many hours to complete, with the stated goal of improving self-verification and long-context management. The timing is notable. Grok 4.7 arrived less than two weeks after Anthropic closed out a run of three Claude 5.5-family releases, and just days after Mistral unveiled its open-weight Large 4 model. For developers choosing a default coding assistant, October 2026 has turned into the most crowded release window of the year, with SpaceXAI, Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, and Mistral all shipping within a roughly six-week span. ## What Changed: Pricing, Context Window and Coding Benchmarks The headline number out of the Grok 4.7 launch is a coding-benchmark jump. On CursorBench 4.0, a separate benchmark focused on IDE-integrated coding workflows, Grok 4.7 improved from 40.4% to 46.3%. The model also posted a score of 1,657 on Briefcase, an agentic task-completion benchmark, though SpaceXAI did not publish a direct prior-generation comparison for that metric. LLMs.content: [SHATERED](https://shattered.io/) [Hardware & Chips](https://shattered.io/hardware/) # Nace.AI Opens Drex 1.5: 9B Model Scores 58.08 [2026] ![](https://shattered.io/wp-content/uploads/avatars/tvance.webp) [Tom Vance](https://shattered.io/author/tvance/) Updated Oct 11, 2026 · 15 min read Nace.AI has open-sourced Drex 1.5, a decision model built to score options instead of writing paragraphs. The company published the weights on September 28, 2026, and the release has since been picked up across AI trade press as a notable entry in the growing field of small, task-specific models built for enterprise pipelines rather than chat windows. The headline number is 58.08, the score Drex 1.5 posted on Decision Index 0.3.1, a benchmark built around choosing, ranking, and judging rather than generating prose. Nace.AI says that result makes Drex 1.5 the top-ranked model under 10 billion parameters on that board. An earlier version of the same benchmark, Decision Index 0.3.1, put Drex 1.5 in first place under 10B parameters, according to [AI Daily Post’s coverage of the release](https://aidailypost.com/news/nace-ai-open-sources-9b-parameter). LLMs.content: [Skip to content](#main-content) [News](/) English ![Microsoft launches Decision-1 model for fast, structured AI decision-making](/_next/image?url=https%3A%2F%2Fnews.lavx.hu%2Fapi%2Fmedia%2Ffile%2Fmicrosoft-launches-decision-1-model-for-fast-structured-ai-decision-making-1_1791706106320-1200x630.jpg&w=3840&q=75) #AI # Microsoft launches Decision-1 model for fast, structured AI decision-making • ![Elena Varga](/_next/image?url=%2Fauthors%2Felena-varga.webp&w=64&q=75) [Elena Varga](/author/elena-varga) •3 min read Share this article Microsoft released Microsoft-Decision-1, a purpose-built decision-scoring model that outperforms LLMs and competing decision models on latency and accuracy across 36 benchmarks. The model is available now in Microsoft Foundry and OpenRouter. Microsoft introduced Microsoft-Decision-1 on Thursday, a new model designed for structured decision tasks that delivers calibrated probability scores through a simple API call. The model runs in Microsoft Foundry and on OpenRouter. Unlike large language models built for text generation, decision models produce structured outputs that software can act on immediately — routing, classification, prioritization, verification, and workflow control. Microsoft-Decision-1 achieved the highest accuracy in a 36-benchmark comparison spanning nearly 150,000 questions kept blind from training. It measured 2.5 times faster than H2O-Lightning-4B v1.1, the next-fastest competitor, and 35 times faster than GPT-6 Sol. The model post-trains Qwen3.5-9B for single-pass decision scoring. Microsoft plans to rebase it on Microsoft AI and OpenAI models. It supports yes/no, multiple-choice, and rating options, plus rubric-based grading of AI responses and agent actions. Microsoft addressed five core challenges in development. Speed: each decision adds latency in sequential workflows; Decision-1 cuts P50 latency to roughly 35 times faster than GPT-6 Sol. Quality: evaluation across dozens of blinded benchmarks covering routing, ranking, long context, multilingual, out-of-distribution, reasoning, and safety tasks showed strong generalization. Robustness: the model changes its decision on 1.3 percent of perturbed requests on average, with zero flips when option descriptions are paraphrased or reordered. Calibration: a 90 percent prediction is correct about nine times out of ten on representative cases. Safety: testing on 5,250 requests across 11 benchmarks covering harmful content, jailbreaks, and prompt injection showed effective refusal without over-blocking. Internal deployments demonstrate practical impact. Xbox Research processed more than 10,000 open-ended feedback pieces from surveys, Steam, and X, sorting them into researcher-defined themes. The team found Decision-1 competitive with GPT-6 Sol on quality while running over 14 times faster and 200 times cheaper. The Copilot team measured chat and agentic response quality, finding Decision-1 competitive with GPT-5.6 Luna at 100 times the speed. On-call engineers used it for knowledge retrieval across logs, tickets, calls, and messages during live incidents, where it outperformed LLMs on speed and accuracy. Microsoft Discovery applied it to adaptive replanning in scientific experiments, achieving 46 times more consistent scoring than LLM-based approaches at three times the speed, yielding nearly four times faster replanning overall. Microsoft suggests use cases including agent control, model routing, skill-based decisions, data labeling, AI judging, intent analysis, incident routing, data validation, recommendations, search relevance, content classification, code scanning, safety screening, computer and UI use, robotics, and scientific discovery screening. Developers can access Microsoft-Decision-1 in [Microsoft Foundry](https://ai.azure.com/catalog/models/Microsoft-Decision-1) and [OpenRouter](https://openrouter.ai/microsoft/microsoft-decision-1). To receive new posts and support my work, consider becoming a free or paid subscriber. ## 📝 Editorial: Billions in Funding, Hundreds of Papers, One Big Leap? AI’s weekly news cycle increasingly resembles two competitions running in parallel: researchers compete to improve intelligence, while investors compete to price its future. This week, Reflection and Mistral supplied new models, TypeSafe supplied another spectacular financing, and Arena supplied a reminder that someone must measure what all this intelligence does. Together, they suggest a market developing interesting ambitions beyond a better chatbot. Reflection introduced Beam, a mixture-of-experts model with 501 billion parameters, of which 23 billion activate per token. Its technical story centers on reinforcement learning and inference efficiency: Reflection reports generating more than 100 million training rollouts and achieving competitive reasoning performance with substantially less estimated inference compute than some larger rivals. Those estimates are not measured deployment costs, and the weights remain promised for later this month. Still, the proposition matters: agents that execute lengthy workflows need intelligence with an operating budget. Mistral offered a European counterpart with Large 4, nicknamed Le Chonk. The trillion-parameter multimodal model entered public API preview, with weights scheduled for release by month’s end. Mistral emphasizes coding, cybersecurity, finance, and law, alongside training on infrastructure it operates in Europe. My reading is that sovereignty is becoming a product feature. For an enterprise, choosing a model also means choosing who controls deployment, customization, and continued access. An impressive benchmark cannot answer those questions. OpenAI added a more fundamental dimension: intelligence contributing to mathematical discovery. The company released more than 700 manuscripts from an unreleased model, reporting progress on open research problems and supplying Lean formalizations for a portion of the results. Verification remains unfinished, and several manuscripts have already been corrected or withdrawn. That distinction matters: generating a plausible proof and establishing mathematical knowledge are different achievements. Yet the possibility is extraordinary. AI could accelerate research enough that checking, interpreting, and connecting its results becomes a central bottleneck. Arena’s question—can we trust what the model did?—suddenly extends from enterprise workflows to the foundations of science. TypeSafe’s $870 million Series A, led by Andreessen Horowitz at a $7.5 billion valuation, put a price on a different architectural bet. Its Jev model produces typed decisions with confidence estimates that software can consume directly. Consider the thousands of small judgments inside a business process: classify this request, select a tool, escalate this exception. These decisions offer a plausible market for specialized intelligence. The valuation assumes that market will be enormous. According to the company, users can analyze business data and produce visual content using natural-language prompts, without writing code. Alongside the new features, Anthropic has made its office productivity tools — Claude Docs, Slides and Design — generally available to users across all subscription plans following a period of beta testing. The move brings Anthropic into the office software market dominated by Microsoft and Google. Claude Dashboards connects directly to internal enterprise data platforms and customer relationship management (CRM) systems. Users can enter questions or requests in everyday language, and the tool automatically generates live data dashboards and analytical reports. The feature is initially available as a beta service to paid subscribers. ![Claude Dashboards automatically generates live data dashboards and analytical reports from natural-language prompts. (Source: Claude’s X account)](https://cdn.thelec.net/news/photo/202610/14516_14783_4423.jpg) Claude Dashboards automatically generates live data dashboards and analytical reports from natural-language prompts. (Source: Claude’s X account) Claude Motion is a tool for creating editable animations and exporting them as video files. A beta version is available to customers on Team and Enterprise plans. Anthropic previously introduced dashboards that automatically refresh using connected data through live artifacts in Claude Cowork, its desktop AI agent, and artifacts in Claude Code. The new Dashboards and Motion features extend those capabilities to users without programming expertise. ![Claude Docs, Slides and Design are now generally available.](https://cdn.thelec.net/news/photo/202610/14516_14784_4754.jpg) Claude Docs, Slides and Design are now generally available. The ability to visualize data through natural-language prompts in Claude is also expected to affect established data visualization software providers. Business intelligence (BI) products such as Tableau, owned by Salesforce, and Microsoft Power BI have long emphasized drag-and-drop tools for building charts. If users can instead create dashboards by asking Claude questions in natural language, the value of those features could diminish. The shift could also affect licensing models that charge customers based on the number of users. However, enterprise deployments must still meet requirements for consistent metric definitions through a semantic layer, access controls, audit trails and large-scale data processing. If AI-generated dashboards require additional work to verify numerical accuracy, established BI platforms are likely to remain in use for executive reporting and regulatory compliance. Existing BI tools also offer AI capabilities of their own. Even so, Claude could provide an alternative for companies seeking to add BI capabilities with an emphasis on AI rather than specialized software tools. ![Hyun-Seon,...

first five-year plan places artificial intelligence and computing infrastructure at the heart of the city’s next stage of development. Its success, however, will depend less on the scale of the technology than on the quality of its applications, governance and social inclusion. ![](https://www.chinadailyhk.com/upload/main/image/2026/08/03/5c13818d6c9ff09b500032203c8cde21.jpg)The plan has sent an unmistakable message: AI is no longer treated merely as a research topic or a promising area of innovation but positioned as a core industry and a tool for reshaping the economy. It calls for continued advancement of the “AI+” initiative, development of computing infrastructure, expansion of digital government, and wider application of AI across finance, trade, logistics, professional services, healthcare, and other public sectors. It also proposes developing the Sandy Ridge Data Facility Cluster, which is expected to begin operation by 2029 and eventually provide computing capacity equivalent to about 36 times Hong Kong’s current level. The decisive question is whether the city can turn computing power into productive, trusted and inclusive applications. Open Source AI.content: # Cryptomining malware used poetry to infect more than 3,400 servers, researchers say — four words in the PoeLLM verse, changed 11 times, point the botnet to new servers Likeliest path into LiteLLM servers was a bug with a fix since April. Over 3,400 “victim servers” were hit by cryptomining malware PoeLLM during a campaign named Canto Incognito, tracked since April 2026, Lumen’s cybersecurity research team Black Lotus Labs reports. The malware’s “command-and-control (C2) mechanism” used address encoding through four words in a two-stanza poem on GitHub, altered 11 times so far, to direct affected hosts to new C2 servers. Most of those hit look to be running “vulnerable versions of open-source AI/LLM services, such as LiteLLM and Ollama,” despite an April LiteLLM fix that probably patched the exploitation path. The malware’s payload consists of XMRig and Iron miners, connected to Kryptex mining infrastructure, with infected servers becoming scanners and exploit servers. The “primary commonality amongst the first 900 victims” was contact with “an endpoint for the Russian crypto mining service,” Lumen says. This indicates that it may be financially motivated. “AI infrastructure is becoming an attractive target” because exposed AI services may contain valuable data and hardware access, especially GPUs. In the meantime, it has “blocked all traffic to and from the PoeLLM C2 servers.” The primary targets are LiteLLM, a proxy server (AI Gateway) to call LLM APIs, a way companies can route their apps to many models through one endpoint, and Gotenberg, a Docker-based API for PDF conversion, which has a guide warning not to expose it to the internet. Also hit are Ollama, which allows you to run open-weight models on your own hardware, although it is not internet-exposed by default, and Gitea, a self-hosted Git platform. Ivanti Sentry, an enterprise gateway appliance, “may also have been targeted,” and one instance was how Lumen discovered the campaign. Although the malware’s methodology involves leveraging poetry, this is only for pointing the infected servers to the C2 server. It is not a form of an AI jailbreak through harmful requests or prompt injection, or what is known as “adversarial poetry,” described in a paper last year. The poem, “On the Nature of Connection,” was first committed in April, with each new version pointing to a new C2 server. The malware is able to decode the new address by pulling specific words and converting them into an IPv4 address. Lumen says that “the malware creator has not changed the pattern used in deciphering the poem” at the time of reporting. Using a poem likely aided in obfuscation as it is “a perfect vehicle for hiding an important message,” the researchers told The Register. The malware is “deployed through vulnerability exploitation of publicly exposed services,” with broad scanning beginning in May. For LiteLLM, a crafted POST to the connection endpoint “was likely the exploitation path,” based on a flaw where two endpoints would run a supplied command on the host with no role check (CVE-2026-42271), which CISA added to its list of exploited vulnerabilities in June. Lumen didn’t detail the methods for Ollama, Gotenberg, and Gitea. If you want to check your own systems, look at connection logs for the indicators of compromise listed on Lumen’s GitHub page. Be sure to audit external exposure when installing any open-source tool and close unnecessary ports. Patch any and all network devices. Follow the individual advisories for the vulnerable products — LiteLLM 1.83.7 or later and Ivanti Sentry R10.5.2, R10.6.2, or R10.7.1. Open Source AI.content: [Skip to content](#main-content) [News](/) English #AI # Torvalds says he "really likes using AI" as Linux community debates LLM rules • ![Elena Varga](/_next/image?url=%2Fauthors%2Felena-varga.webp&w=64&q=75) [Elena Varga](/author/elena-varga) •4 min read Share this article Linus Torvalds has waded into the Linux community's debate over AI-generated code and contributions, saying he "really likes using AI" for development work, even as maintainers weigh new rules around LLM-generated content. Linus Torvalds has weighed in on one of the Linux kernel community's most contentious debates: how to handle AI-generated code and contributions. Speaking as the project's longtime leader, Torvalds said he "really likes using AI" for his own development work, a statement that lands in the middle of an ongoing discussion among maintainers about whether and how to regulate LLM-generated patches. The debate isn't hypothetical. Kernel maintainers have been fielding an increasing volume of patches that appear to be generated or heavily assisted by large language models. Some of these contributions are useful; others are low-quality noise that wastes reviewer time. That tension has pushed the community to consider formal rules, including requirements that contributors disclose AI assistance. Torvalds' comments cut through the procedural talk. He didn't position himself as an AI evangelist or a skeptic. He described a practical workflow: he uses AI tools because they help him get work done. That's a notable stance from someone who has built a reputation for blunt, no-nonsense technical judgment. The reaction from the community has been mixed. Some developers see Torvalds' endorsement as a signal that AI-assisted development is here to stay and that the kernel project should adapt. Others worry that his influence could steer the conversation away from the disclosure requirements some maintainers want. ## What the community is actually arguing about The core question isn't whether AI tools are useful. Most developers who have tried modern coding assistants agree they can speed up boilerplate work, suggest reasonable patterns, and help with unfamiliar APIs. The friction comes from accountability and quality control. A human contributor who submits a patch can explain their reasoning, defend their design choices, and iterate on feedback. An AI-generated patch arrives with no such context. Reviewers have to reverse-engineer the intent behind the code, which is harder when the submitter themselves may not fully understand what the model produced. There's also the volume problem. LLMs make it cheap to generate plausible-looking code at scale. A single person can flood a mailing list with dozens of patches that look superficially reasonable but fail under scrutiny. That's a real burden on a volunteer review corps that already has more work than time. Some maintainers have proposed mandatory disclosure: if you used AI to write or substantially assist with a patch, say so. Others argue that disclosure requirements are unenforceable and that the review process should judge the code on its merits regardless of how it was produced. ## Torvalds' practical take Torvalds didn't engage with the policy debate directly in his remarks. He spoke as a developer who has found genuine utility in the tools. His framing suggests he sees AI as another tool in the kit, not a category of contribution that needs special handling. That perspective carries weight. The Linux kernel is one of the largest and most rigorously reviewed software projects in existence. If its leader finds AI assistance genuinely useful for his own work, that's a data point other developers will weigh heavily. It also complicates the case for strict disclosure rules. If the project's most prominent developer is using AI tools as part of his normal workflow, drawing a clean line between "human-written" and "AI-assisted" code becomes even harder. Open Source AI.content: [Real-time News](/topics/Latest) [Watchlist](/watchlist)[Holdings](/stocklist)[Market](/market)[Earnings Call](/earnings-call)[Event Calendar](/calendar)[Podcast](/podcast) ![](https://img.youtube.com/vi/qFaKvbVc5cE/hqdefault.jpg) [Teaching Agents to Search with NVIDIA Data Designer — Dhruv Nathawani, NVIDIA](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qFaKvbVc5cE) GuestDhruv Nathawani 4 hours ago00:55:13en ![](/images/img_default_profile@2x.png)[AI Engineer](/podcast?source=AI%20Engineer) ## Key Takeaways NVIDIA's Dhruv Nathawani demonstrates Data Designer for building synthetic search-agent training data, showing Wikidata-seeded riddles and Tavily trajectories lifted Nemotron Nano's BrowseComp score from 0 to 30 percent. ## Summary The most useful thing in this 55-minute workshop is not the headline topic of "teaching agents to search" — that is the final third of the talk. Most of the session is a working tutorial on NVIDIA's open-source **Data Designer** framework for synthetic data generation, and the search case study is the payoff that demonstrates the method. The central claim, made by NVIDIA research scientist Dhruv Nathawani, is that the hard part of building agent capabilities is not the model but the data pipeline: you take a target agent behavior, turn it into a data problem, generate diverse synthetic data grounded in real-world seeds, filter it aggressively, and only then train. His headline result: using this approach, NVIDIA moved its Nemotron model from 0% to 30% on the BrowseComp search benchmark, and from 26% to 41% on the Bird text-to-SQL benchmark. Nathawani walks through three notebooks — Data Designer basics, Model Context Protocol (MCP) tool-calling data, and end-to-end agentic search — and is candid that he "blazed through" the first two because the search notebook is the crux. He also spends the last stretch on a topic he says is genuinely unsolved: how to evaluate synthetic data, illustrated by a concrete failure where his own Wikidata seed had gone stale. The reader should walk away with the framework's abstractions (seed columns, sampler columns, LLM columns, LLM-as-judge), the specific numbers behind the Nemotron search dataset, and a clear-eyed view of the evaluation gap. Dhruv Nathawani is a research scientist at NVIDIA and part of the Nemotron team, which builds NVIDIA's open-source foundation models. He presented this as a one-hour workshop (a prior version ran two hours), with notebooks and slides in a public GitHub repo referenced by a recurring QR code. ## Data Designer turns a target agent behavior into a data pipeline The framework's core premise is that internet data is not the data you want for a transformer — a quote Nathawani attributes to Andrej Karpathy — because internet data ranges from high-quality sources like Wikipedia to random opinions on X. The traditional approach is to curate that data; Data Designer's approach is to generate synthetic data either from scratch or from a seed dataset, so the output is "grounded in real-world distribution and real-world data" rather than purely model-invented. Nathawani is explicit about why naive generation fails. If you just loop an LLM a million times asking for a product, a review, and a customer profile, you get repetition after 10–20 iterations, no correlations between features, no multimodality, no steering, no validation, and no way to share the process with a colleague. [Thomas Reid](/author/thomas_reid/) October 11, 202611 min read ![](https://assets.insightmediagroup.io/media/1791463767654_gchmb3.webp) Image by AI I recently covered TypesafeAI’s JEVin TDS (link at the end). JEV makes fast decisions, such as classifying content or choosing the next step in a workflow, and returns typed answers that software can use directly. The accompanying probabilities help an application decide whether to act on an answer or pass it to a person for review. The internet went a bit crazy over JEV, so it was no surprise to see rival products appear after its release. Among the most prominent was the Decisions API that OpenAI previewed at its recent DevDay and made available as a public beta shortly after. In this article, I’ll look at the new API, how to get it, and some practical use-case examples, and I’ll let you know whether I think it’s a JEV killer or whether TypesafeAI can sleep soundly at night. ## The background to JEV-like models Suppose you run an online shop. A customer writes to say that their keyboard arrived with three broken keys and asks for a replacement. Before anyone replies, your application needs to decide which team should handle the message. You could ask a language model to classify it and return JSON. But the application only needs a category and enough information to decide whether to trust that category. That process could also be relatively slow and costly if it had to handle 1000s of requests. OpenAI’s Decisions API gives that operation its own endpoint. Additionally, OpenAI claims its Decisions API can make decisions up to ten times faster than GPT-6 Luna, the LLM that Decisions is based on, through the Responses API. To explore how it works, we’ll walk through three Python examples and compare OpenAI’s approach with TypesafeAI’s JEV model. One major advantage of the Decisions API over JEV is that it can handle images. We’ll see an example of that later. ## What the OpenAI Decisions API returns A request supplies a model, some input and a list of questions. The current beta supports the **gpt-6-luna** LLM. Questions share the input, which can contain text, images or both. There are three question types: plaintext ``` +-----------+--------------------------------------------------+------------------------------+ | Type | Question | Result | +-----------+--------------------------------------------------+------------------------------+ | predicate | Does the document contain a return deadline? | A probability between zero | | | | and one | +-----------+--------------------------------------------------+------------------------------+| choice | Which support queue should receive this message? | A selected value, | | | | probabilities and confidence | +-----------+--------------------------------------------------+------------------------------+ | score | How severely does this incident affect customers?| A score across ordered || | | levels, probabilities and | | | | confidence | +-----------+--------------------------------------------------+------------------------------+ ``` These fields are defined in the SDK’s response types. A predicate doesn’t return a Boolean: your code chooses the threshold that turns its probability into an action. The API returns answers in question order. It can also refuse individual questions, so check an answer’s **type** before reading its other fields. Defining the available answers is part of designing the application. Infra & Chips.content: # NVIDIA’s CUDA Moat Is Accelerating RTX Spark Laptop Sales, Higher 128GB Unified Memory Options Belonging To Surface Laptop Ultra Already Out Of Stock [Omar Sohail](https://wccftech.com/author/omarsohail/) • [Comments](#comments "View comments") [Add to Preferres Sources](javascript:void(0)) Microsoft’s product page for the [Surface Laptop Ultra](https://wccftech.com/microsoft-teases-rtx-spark-powered-surface-laptop-ultra-starting-at-2599/) shows the [RTX Spark](https://wccftech.com/nvidia-enters-pc-space-with-rtx-spark/), 128GB unified memory, and 1TB SSD configuration priced at $5,899.99 is already listed as out of stock. While the lower-tier options are up for grabs, it indicates that the sellout may partly reflect limited early supply, but that’s unconfirmed because Microsoft hasn’t shared any data. However, the demand behind these RTX Spark laptops makes sense when you sit down to contemplate that these machines are tailor-made for a bigger user base, and a lot has to do with CUDA support. ## The full NVIDIA software stack, tackling a multitude of workloads, is a prime factor why RTX Spark laptops are picking up in popularity With the unified memory architecture (UMA) paired with NVIDIA’S RTX platform and full CUDA support, developers and creators already tied into heavy workflows will find machines like the Surface Laptop Ultra incredibly useful. Most AI frameworks, inference engines, and creative tools are written and optimized for CUDA first, so buyers can run their existing software stack without hunting for workarounds. [##### **Related Story** ASUS Markets Its RTX Spark-Powered ProArt GR1X Mini-PCs As Efficient Gaming Powerhouses, Can Run 1440p Titles At 100FPS With Just A 140W Power Limit](https://wccftech.com/asus-proart-gr1x-rtx-spark-mini-pc-1440p-100fps-140w/) Sure, rival platforms like AMD’s [Ryzen AI MAX 400](https://wccftech.com/amd-pushes-ryzen-ai-max-400-to-192gb-memory-single-chip-run-300b-ai-llms-locally/) can offer large memory pools of up to 192GB, but few can match that software compatibility. For professionals, time lost to tooling is more costly than spending a small fortune on premium hardware. Previously, NVIDIA’s fastest consumer-grade GPU shipped with 32GB of VRAM. With the RTX Spark, that memory count has reached 128GB and is dynamically shared between CPU and GPU. NVIDIA has claimed that it’s possible to run 120B AI models with up to a one million Context Window, making RTX Spark laptops incredibly attractive to developers, researchers, and companies handling sensitive data that want to run large models privately and avoid recurring cloud costs. Since the top configuration of the Surface Laptop Ultra offers this unified memory headroom, it explains why it’s the one that sold out first. That’s not to say that there aren’t any trade-offs with RTX Spark laptops, with the most glaring one being memory bandwidth. At just 273GB/s, the Surface Laptop Ultra pales in comparison with something like the M5 Max MacBook Pro, which, at the same 128GB unified RAM count, boasts up to a whopping 614GB/s bandwidth, which can become the difference in workloads dependent on increased throughput. For example, the laptop version of the RTX 5090 handily beats the M5 Max in both prompt processing and token generation with up to a [133 percent performance increase in LLM benchmarks](https://wccftech.com/rtx-5090-laptop-vs-m5-max-llm-benchmarks/) thanks to its 896GB/s memory bandwidth. Unfortunately, it falls short in running the denser models thanks to its 24GB GDDR7 VRAM limitation. This is where the RTX Spark shines, with NVIDIA’s CUDA ecosystem locking in a plethora of users. Infra & Chips.content: Amazon recently followed Microsoft’s lead and said it will no longer use nondisclosure agreements (NDAs) while negotiating with local governments over data centers. On the latest episode of TechCrunch’s Equity podcast, Sean O’Kane, Rebeccan Bellan and I discussed Amazon’s announcement, which came in the middle of a longer blog post making the case that data centers are actually good for communities. Rebecca was a bit skeptical that the recent spate of data center moratoriums will have a lasting effect, especially since the moratoriums only last for a year or two and “these data centers aren’t coming online for the next two, three, four, five years,” though I countered that data center backers definitely seem worried. Sean, meanwhile, suggested that a big reason for the backlash is the industry’s poor communication. “We’ve seen, through a lot of the controversy and backlash to AI and data centers, that the industry just does a really poor job explaining itself, and that they are obviously and constantly frustrated with the fact that most people can’t envision a world in which this stuff is useful for them,” he said. Keep reading for a preview of our conversation, edited for length and clarity. Sean O’Kane: It’s an interesting thing that it was sort of buried in the blog post and part of a larger story that Amazon’s clearly trying to tell. I guess I understand why they weren’t putting it in the foreground, but to me, this is at the root of so many of the problems that the tech industry currently faces when it comes to AI broadly, but data centers in particular. There are so many things that could be said about whether or not people should be worried about the effect that data centers have on their property values, on their electricity bills, on their water usage in the area, and whether or not those things are real problems, inflated problems, etc. etc. I think so much of that just really goes back to the fact that a lot of these projects are being negotiated essentially in secret. Sometimes they’re being negotiated [with the public knowing] that it’s a data center, but just not knowing who’s actually going to use it or occupy it at any point. This is a long-standing issue with the tech industry. I always go back to the mid-2010s when Uber was expanding really fast. Uber was one of the companies that really used this tactic a ton when it came to working with local governments. In particular, I remember I was working at The Verge at the time and we had a freelancer write a story about a city outside of Orlando where Uber was trying to negotiate tax subsidies to subsidize rides for people to use public transit after the Uber trip. The whole thing was negotiated in secret. And not only that, which was frustrating on its face, but also, because of the secrecy, you could just see Uber getting really comfortable with asking for a lot of other stuff, too. So there needs to be more of this. I’m glad Amazon’s doing this. We’ll see if it actually does have any positive effect, but people are pretty entrenched right now. Rebecca Bellan: Yeah, I’m curious about what effect this will have and whether it will lead to communities successfully delaying or or killing any infrastructure that the companies need to build. What I’ve heard from some people I’ve spoken to, who deal with data centers every day, a lot of these moratoriums that are getting passed — and there are a significant number of them, including one recently in San Francisco, which is pretty ironic — but they’re only for like a year or two years. But these data centers aren’t coming online for the next two, three, four, five years. All of the buildouts are going to be massively delayed for a number of reasons from zoning to funding. Of course, if the pushback keeps going, then it might have an effect, but I often wonder just how much of an effect this political pushback is having on this. Infra & Chips.content: # Learning to use local AI is exciting, overwhelming, and frustrating It’s like using cloud-based AI tools, but the privacy makes it more appealing.﻿ # Learning to use local AI is exciting, overwhelming, and frustrating It’s like using cloud-based AI tools, but the privacy makes it more appealing.﻿ I’m embarking on a journey I’ve so far been hesitant to go on: actually using AI on the regular. Giving my most personal data to cloud services has been a major hold up for me, but it’s increasingly possible to run powerful models locally to see what they’re capable of. Is this tech so useful that it’s worth throwing gobs of money at a computer or a laptop with lots of overpriced RAM? I’ll try to help you find out. I’m not an AI expert, it’s going to be a journey for me, but maybe I can help you see if that journey is worth taking — and I’ll be posting my way through it. A big part of Apple’s pitch for its new Mac desktops is how good they are for local AI, and there’s an entire line of new RTX Spark Windows machines landing imminently with up to 128GB of RAM aimed at using agentic AI. Local AI and agents are just, like, so hot right now. But, in all seriousness, the thought of having a little gofer living solely in the box on my desk that answers only to me and not overlords from OpenAI, Google, Microsoft, or Anthropic hits a bit different than trusting cloud services or subscribing to a chatbot. Don’t get me wrong, there’s still no way I’m gonna have it write for me, edit for me, or generate ugly fliers. But now, with some privacy on my side maybe I can finally think of useful busy work to “trust” it with. So as part of my ongoing testing of the M5 Ultra Mac Studio, as well as experimenting on other Mac and Windows systems, I’ve installed some local LLMs and I’m beginning to tinker. Here’s how things are going. I started by installing the open-source Hermes Agent on the Mac Studio. Hermes is a self-hosted AI agent desktop app that works on macOS, Windows, and Linux. It’s completely free to use if you stick to local LLMs. Since this M5 Ultra Mac Studio has 256GB of unified memory, I could run just about any model I want. This is how things quickly get overwhelming. There are more models out there than I can count, and some have specialized uses. Generally, models with many billions of parameters are able to do more than smaller ones with only a few billion. And since we don’t have to worry about paying for tokens when running a model locally, I figured I’d go big to start. Using Hermes’ straightforward onboarding interface and model picker, I chose the Qwen 3.8 Flash Next model — a 125-billion parameter model that’s around 105GB in size. I also plan on spending some time with much smaller Qwen models on devices like an M6 Mac Mini, M5 MacBook Air, an Asus TUF Gaming A14 with AMD Strix Halo processor, and, eventually, RTX Spark. (Care to share what local models and hardware you use? You know where to leave your comments. 🫡) It wasn’t long to get up and running with Hermes and Qwen, and even make them controllable via my phone by using a Telegram bot. But then, I was presented with my usual nemesis when it comes to using AI: the text box. “What do I do with this thing?” First up, to get things going, I followed some helpful YouTube advice and had Hermes make me a daily morning briefing — to just start small with a cron job and ensure things are working. It scans my email and calendar, tells me anything worth my immediate attention, and gives me a short weather report. It’s not all that useful, and you obviously don’t need a $12,000 computer to build it, but it’s something I can develop over time. The brief kept failing to generate at first, but then I eventually figured out that macOS couldn’t be asleep when the job fired up at 7:30am. Duh! It works like clockwork now, but I have to think of more info for it to pull for me to make the results more helpful. A more useful task was reorganizing my Steam library. I have over 400 games o...
